utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you told us last week 25 more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may have been clear, but just to make it absolutely certain, did that number include the witnesses who we are hearing this week or is it 25 after Easter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe when I gave you that estimate, Your Honour, that was not including the witnesses we have now heard this week. But there were some other witnesses, and perhaps it was a rather presumptuous statement to make, in the sense that I did not include the number of transcript witnesses. And I realise in retrospect that -- what I did say, I believe, was viva voce witnesses, provided the Court doesn't -- I realise that there has yet a ruling to be made on those witnesses, and some of those witnesses may in fact be cross-examined by the Defence, but my estimate of 25 was -- at that point we had about 25 more witnesses. Now, we've been cutting some of them back and we have actually stricken or struck some of the witnesses from our list in order to try to meet our June 1st target date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you give us an up-to-date figure, then, this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I certainly can, at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have about 29 working days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why we're -- I worked till 11.00 last night getting summaries ready to make sure we could have another witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your industry is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Have summaries been circulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Whilst we're waiting for the witness, I haven't given my usual note to my learned friend as to what he can lead on as far as the Defence of Sikirica is concerned, but it's paragraphs 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if my other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic -- Mr. Petrovic, rather, and Mr. Vucicevic, would you indicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in respect of this witness, we believe that this witness can be led only on the general data, which means all the way to his arrest; after that, I think that the witness needs to be examined directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with what Mr. Petrovic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, sir, I understand that you were born and raised in Bosanski Petrovac, where you attended school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you're presently 55 years old?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm 56 already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And I understand, sir, that after you attended school, you went on to study education until that was interrupted by your compulsory service in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. It was teachers' faculty. I was to be a teacher of physics and technical training, and there is an explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I believe perhaps it's --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia, where you use the word "education," it means something else. An educator is somebody who specialises in psychological work with children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Then it's my use of terminology, sir, but is it safe to say that, after you served your compulsory service, you graduated in 1973 as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Teacher of physics and technical training.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that for us, sir. Now, sir, you taught at a school in Kozarac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. It is correct. For the past 15 or 16 years, yes. But before that, I worked in Omarska first, then at Lamovita. After that, for about two school years in Lamovita, I did not last more than two school years, my work in Lamovita, and then I went to Kozarac and I spent the rest of my career in the school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Focusing on your career as a teacher in Kozarac, I understand that that's where you were working as a teacher in the years leading up to 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it safe to say that at that school, your colleagues, there were some 130 some odd teachers there at the time. You are nodding your head, meaning yes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And is it also safe to say, sir, that the ethnic composition of those teachers was mixed? There were, like, 30 per cent Serbs, there was some Croats and Ukranians, and the rest were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I mean 30 per cent -- well, nobody really counted, but, yes, that would roughly be their share, yes. The majority, yes, they were Muslims, that is, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right. And just so that I am clear, you, sir, consider yourself to be of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No; a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Muslim -- no, I'm sorry, but a Muslim means your religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Are you able to tell us what your particular religious affiliation is, sir?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Islamic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand that about 90 per cent of the children who attended your school were also of the Islamic faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, do I understand that many of the male teachers in your school, prior to the outbreak of the war, were in the JNA reserve, regardless of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were different types of reserve. They have all or, rather, the majority of our men had gone through the regular military service, which was 11 or 12 months of the officers' school, that is. And the regular troops, well, it depended on their profession, that is, a year and a half or 16 months or something like that. And -- but then they could be divided; there was Territorial Defence, and civil defence, and all this was within the JNA and, to us, it was all legitimate and lawful, and the majority of people attended the drills, the exercises, exercises which lasted three days or five days or perhaps longer or perhaps on Saturdays, which were days off.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure that I need quite as much detail concerning -- is it just fair to say that many of the male teachers were in the JNA reserve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is correct. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, no, just -- perhaps I will just skip on, sir. I understand that at some point you noticed a change in the type of broadcasts that were available on Radio Prijedor, the newspaper, Kozarski Vijesnik, and the Banja Luka TV; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is, but not that simple, and not that short. The -- there were different kinds of changes, and it started before 1990. But I suppose we don't have time for any more detailed explanations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn your mind to whether there were any changes that were readily apparent shortly before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question. I mean, could you please explain it to -- your question better. Changes in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in my school, in my work organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, in the media. In other words -- let me rephrase it. Did you --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, media.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Did you see a radical change in the media in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Indeed, I did, and out of the blue in 1990 -- 1992, yes, those changes were very abrupt, and in a way, they killed off normal men, and I consider myself a normal man. I mean propaganda of different sorts, aggressive propaganda divided along ethnic lines. As for Prijedor, Prijedor itself, one could feel it in Prijedorski Glas, and I also read regularly and also read Politika Ekspres and Belgrade dailies. I made some comparisons. Prijedor Radio, Banja Luka television, when the radio station in Kozarac was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Those were drastic changes already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Without getting into the detail about those changes, sir, I'm going to ask whether, at some point, you stopped teaching school in Kozarac and, if so, why did you stop going to classes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I stopped going to classes because on the last day that I spent in Kozarac, and it was the 25th or the 26th of May, and to be quite frank, for the past five, six, ten days, I was trying to avoid, that is, I used the car or I rode a bus or other -- and I road a bus because I dared not take out my car. And the 25th, I think that was the last day that I was there, was the Thursday or Friday, I don't know, but that was the last time that I was in Kozarac, that I went to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were trying to avoid something or you took your car out. What were you trying to avoid?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: There were -- up at Orlovci, which is about a kilometre, perhaps two, away there were already guards, Serbs stood guard there. That was in the early days. Then, there was a small bridge at the entrance to Susici, we called it the next locality, there is a small bridge there. And then up by the petrol pump at the entrance into Kozarac, there was yet another guard, because the situation was not normal, and there was a kind of a combination, as far as I could gather. People from Kozarac, something mixed, some Serbs together with -- I did not really follow it very much because all of that did not look normal to me. It smelled of evil, and I was afraid and I heard some criticisms from my colleagues, objections, "Oh, you are still going there, I daren't." And that is why I eventually stopped going to work in Kozarac one of those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I understand, sir, between the 25th or 26th of May - which was the last days you say that you remember going to school as a teacher - and the 23rd of June, what is it you did? What did you do between near the end of May to near the end of June?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Between the end of May, well, all that time -- mostly, except on the 23rd of June, most of that time I spent in the flat because I realised it all. I was not politically committed, involved either before, or then, or now. My area of interest, my intellectual needs are different and I believe I am entitled to them. And between the 26th -- no, the 25th and it was Monday, if I remember well, I went out to buy newspapers. At that time, I used to buy four or five different papers. In the former Yugoslavia at that time, all the papers from all over were available, so I bought the papers and I bought a carton of cigarettes, that is, ten packages. I went out in my sweatsuit, and I walked around Patria, around that side of the theatre, and there was a checkpoint of sorts. And I was wearing this sweatsuit which was checkered, something blue and green, or something like that. And then a guard halted me, "Identity card, here you are. What do you need this for? It is a Croat flat. It is a Ustasha flag, zenga, by the wall." At that time, I didn't really know, well, I knew roughly what the old Croatian flag looked, it was red and white checkers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to the interpretation. The witness said that, in part, he was colour-blind and that is missing from the translation.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I am mixing up red and green. Everybody who knows what that means will understand. For instance, when I see traffic lights, I can identify them. When it comes to nuances, I cannot tell them apart, but I know what is blue. I know what is black. I know what is white. And these are the characteristic -- this is very characteristic of color-blind persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, but for this one occasion when you went out to get newspapers, is it fair to say, sir, that you stayed in your flat for most of the time between the 25th of May and the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I never left my apartment until the arrest -- the flat, no. The yard, outside the yard, no. I was with my neighbours. But I never left the flat, the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you not leave the flat of the building because of that experience that you have just related to us about being checked by a guard when you went to buy a newspaper and cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He forced me to lean against a wall, and then some snipers came up, so that he let me go. Otherwise I think that that guard, the guard who was there, it must have been a former pupil of mine, but I am not sure, so I cannot really say. But I suppose he recognised me. And then some confusion ensued and he told me, "F you," and let me go. And then I was in the house until 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening. I simply never left the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's move on, then, to the 23rd of June. You had stayed in your flat after that scary incident, and then on the 23rd of June something happened. What was that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I was reading something in the flat, and then the children, my older daughter, came, and said that the police wanted to speak to me, to, that is, come downstairs. And I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps -- I'm going to ask you some questions and direct you to certain areas, with my friends' permission. Sir, I understand that your child came and told you some policemen wanted to see you downstairs. Did you go downstairs?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The police had said -- yes, I did. I did go downstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you got there, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Downstairs.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Where? In front of the building, in the vehicle? Well, there were very many children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. Let me be very specific. You were sent downstairs by your child, who said that there was a policeman waiting for you. Is that correct, or am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you got there --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you got there, quite apart from how many children there were, how many policemen were there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: There was one policeman, one soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did. Not well, but a policeman on the beach. We called him Strika. I do not know what his name was, but we've called him Strika for 20 years. A tall man, dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there anyone with him?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: There was a soldier, a young man in a military uniform, in a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you met Strika and this young man in the military uniform, what, if anything, did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. They told me to get into the car, and I asked why. And he said, "You'll learn soon enough." Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: When they brought me to the police station -- we rode to the police station, we entered, and I had my identity card with me. That was the only personal paper that I had on me. And he told me to sit -- there was a bench to the right with a table, a wooden bench. We call it a bench. It's about five -- it would seat five or six. And it was there, and he told me to sit there and wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, the size of the bench probably isn't that significant. What I'm asking you to do is -- you were asked to sit and wait there, were you? Yes.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you wait for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how long did you wait before something happened?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Two hours. I had my watch. Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Then he -- Strika came from somewhere outside, took me into the office - not the first; the second office to the right - and he took my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 particulars, the basic ones, name and the rest, then took me out and made me board a car where there was already -- and there was a woman in it, and then that same soldier, that young man, and Strika was the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the woman who was already in the car when you were placed in it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did, yes. I recognised her. She was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was the name of the woman that you say you know, if you know the name?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Suada. We called her Suada, Suada, conductor Suada. She frequently checked tickets between Prijedor-Kozarac, Prijedor-Omarska. Suada, was it Ramic? I don't know. Suada.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: She was already in the back seat of this car and you were placed in the car and then were you taken somewhere?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: They took me to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, if I can just back up for one moment. Did they search you at all, sir, when they first put you in the car when they picked you up at home?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Up until this point, you were not searched. You were taken to the SUP, which is the police station, you waited for a few hours, and then you were taken by Strika and put in the car and driven to Keraterm; is that the effect of what happened?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you got to Keraterm, sir, what happened to you there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking -- a soldier, I was thinking whether he'll go to Omarska or Keraterm. But Strika, according to them, decided that I should go to Keraterm after all, and he brought me to what we used to call the scales. That was an area with a kiosk and with a brick floor. It was already dark. It was 10 past 9.00, or something like that, in the evening. I saw the troops, military. That was all new to me. Uniformed, half-uniformed, red caps, pistols which the army did not use. They were Zastava pistols. And all of that wasn't very pleasant for me. I was shocked. It was an unpleasant situation. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, but listen to my questions, if you would, please. When you arrived at Keraterm, were you searched?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not sure, because I still cannot recognise him properly, but I think it was Mr. Kajin - that is what he called him - a short man, I mean, to my mind, 176 or something, fat, short sleeves, T-shirt, military uniform, red cap, relatively round-faced. And he searched -- he only frisked me very superficially, because I only had the sweatsuit and a shirt and a watch and identity card, so it did not last long. He just frisked me barely. Nobody beat me there at the entrance, which otherwise happened quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You say that it happened quite often. This is something you found out later during your stay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I watched it often. Practically everybody was beaten, all the groups, most of them. For instance, Brezicani, that's a village from which people also came, were not beaten. That is what I remember. As for others, I think they were all more or less beaten, what I could see, what I saw, what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Witness, just slow down a little, because the interpreters have to interpret everything you're saying. At the speed at which you're saying it, that must be difficult. Did Strika, in your presence, tell the guards anything about what to do or not to do with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: "This one is not dangerous," something like that. "This one is harmless," or something to that effect. "Let him go."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As a result of that, were you beaten when you arrived at Keraterm, sir, when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. No, not then. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment. Where did you go after you were searched? Where were you put or where were you told to go?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kajin -- but I learnt his name later, or rather the guards told me. No, sorry. The prisoners. Mr. Kajin told me to go to Room 1. I didn't know about it, so I asked him where, and he came close to me and said, "Over there," and indicated a room to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you go there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't enter it straight away. I had no time to do it. As I was walking towards the room, unsure of my whereabouts because it was dark, and then Kajin, Mr. Kajin, invited me to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say he invited you, what kinds of words did he use that you interpreted --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: To walk back to him. And when I did, he asked me if I had worked in the Kozarac school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did he ask you anything else?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He then asked me if I knew Medunjali [phoen], or rather he meant Becir Medunjanin. I told him yes, I worked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did this Kajin, or this person that you say was Kajin, say anything to you after you said that you worked with him?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That was an outpour, outburst, which was shocking to me, because I had known that man, had worked for 20 years with that man. I was told that I was something like an advisor to him. There were all sorts of things to that effect, to that effect. But for instance, I remember that he was a fundamentalist. He didn't really know what the word "fundamentalist" means, I suppose, but I realised what that meant within the context of the propaganda, what I had already heard about Medunjanin from the press, from television and the rest, and I was scared. I barely made it to number 1. I was -- I was in cold sweat all over by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just one more question before we break, if I may. You went to Room 1, I understand, sir, and when you got there, were the other detainees in that room interested? What did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, there were very many people there. It was full, and we say full as a matchbox. There was a huge number of people in that area. I simply did not know where was I to put up, where to sit down, how. And then I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was that the question you asked, for a description of the room?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't, Your Honour. Perhaps we should have the break now and I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if the witness understood that he must answer the questions. No doubt you know what you want to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have tried to ask the witness to listen to my question, Your Honour, but I understand that he wants to tell a story. And I'm going to have to attempt to control the amount of detail I'm getting, but I'm a bit constrained by the fact that my friends have indicated they don't want me to lead. But I do want to direct him specifically to the areas of interest, so I'll do that after the break, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he wants to get away today and finish his evidence, the more shortly he answers the questions, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would this be an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be. We will take a break now. Mr. Hidic, we're now going to take an adjournment for half an hour. During the adjournment you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, but my client has had consultation with the registry in between, so I was -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just before the break, you told us that you went -- you were sent to Room 1 after your discussion with Kajin and, upon your arrival, I take it there were other detainees in the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Upon your arrival, did you have a conversation with any of the detainees concerning what you had been doing in relation to just before you came into the room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I recognised a colleague with whom I had worked. There was no seating room, there was only -- standing room only and he asked me, "What had Kajin asked you?" I told him that he had asked me about Becir Medunjanin and to this he said what it was. I mentioned about the fundamentalist and his advisor issue and then Namik said that there was no worse accusation in Keraterm than that one. This is what Namik said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When your colleague said to you, "What did Kajin ask?" who did you understand him to mean when he said "Kajin"?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question very well. My apologies. That there were no worse accusations in terms of the -- of the camp inmates, their position. My position in relation to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask the question in a different way. You're speaking to your colleague, and as I understood your evidence, you said your colleague said to you, "What did Kajin ask?" Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know who he meant when he said "Kajin"? Do you know who he was referring to when he used that name?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. When he said "Kajin," I did not know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that the first time you heard the name Kajin being used?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did it later become clear to you who Kajin was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: 15 minutes later -- 10, 15, perhaps not even 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that in a moment. Sir, you were about to tell us that when you went into Room 1, that it was extremely crowded. I think you've told us that just before the break; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. What I mean to say, the room was simply overcrowded with people; some were sitting, some were lying, some were standing. Most of them were squatting, but many, many people, given that space.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate a number of detainees in Room 1 when you were sent to it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: At that moment, that is what I felt. Later on, we measured the room by feet, and later on, I got a certain idea how much room there was. And later on when I found my space, I found out how much space I had, that was 20, 25 centimetres, and we were about 300 total. Some were then transferred to other rooms, but there were about 300, 350 men. There was about 50 men the length of the room to the door. So you can do your own math by multiplying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I understand your answer, sir, my answer to my specific question is that your estimate is 300 to 350 men in the room at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Approximately. Quite a few at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You volunteered the fact that you measured the room. Did you measure this --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand that. Did you measure this room with some kind of a measuring device or is this pacing it off or how did you measure the room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, pacing it, and some others also said. And then there were some girders of the ceiling and they were spaced two metres apart. But to me, that wasn't important that it was overcrowded. When I came there, I had no place where to go. And it was also -- the odour was very strong. People were filthy, they were unshaven, there were pallets --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, my question just at the moment -- I'll get to those things later. My question at the moment is: Are you able to give us an estimate of the size of the room after you measured it or after you paced it or after you counted the number of girders? Can you tell the Court now, to the best of your recollection, how large Room 1 was?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately the length was about 15 metres, 15 to 20 by 5 or 6 metres, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Moments ago when I asked you a question about the name Kajin, you said about 15 minutes later you learned something more. Tell us what happened 15 minutes or so after you were placed in Room 1.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kajin called me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you go out?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What did you find once you were outside of the room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I saw him first again -- it was already dark at that time. It may have been 9.00, 9.30. It was about 10 minutes later. I saw some guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what, if anything, happened?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: They were already standing there. Kajin was closer to me. Those two guards were already there. Later on I would learn that that was five, six, seven metres in the direction of the road, within this complex, over towards Room 2. And this is what I saw at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did something happen when you went outside and encountered Kajin and the two guards?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: These guards called me over and immediately beating started.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who beat you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Later on I learnt, even though I had not known them before. They were young men. They were 150, 160, tall, longer hair. I remember that they had military boots. I think that they were wearing military uniform. They first started beating me with rifle butts. That is where I received my first blow, here. I fell down, I got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you demonstrate where "here" was? Did you tell us where you received your first blow?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The first blow came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And for the record, you put your hand to the back of your neck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, behind the neck. That is right. Back of my neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Continue, sir. I didn't mean to interrupt you, but I had to find out for the record where you were struck.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: So he hit me behind the neck. That was one of them. I don't know which one of them it was, even to date. And then these blows went on with rifle butts. I think they had Kalashnikovs. And then it was just general beating. At that point, I could withstand that. And I was an athlete. I know what hitting is. I did some karate in the military. And then -- nothing professional; just as an amateur. So I try to avoid hits as much as I could. Then I fell down. And then I was hit in the crotch. That just fell me. Then I felt fear, then anger. I asked one of these Banovics, "Why are you beating me? What for? What are you beating me for?" One of them, I don't know which one, said, "Do you know that my brother was killed at the front?" I said, "I'm sorry that he was killed, but I did not know about it, and I have nothing to do with it. I'm not guilty of it." Then they went on --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let's stop for a moment --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: -- beating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm just going to clarify a couple of points. In your last narration of what happened to you, you said you asked one of the Banovics. Who are you talking about when you said you asked one of the Banovics? Were they the people that you referred to as the guards earlier or is this someone else?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: These were -- these were the guards. There were three Banovics. I knew one of them, Rade Banovic. He worked with me. And so it wasn't that one, not this person Rade. But later on, I learnt that they were half brothers, that these two were brothers, that they were from my neighbourhood, that they went -- that they hung out with my children. I learnt about their father also later on. But it was those two Banovics who beat me. And something else: I remember also -- that is, while I was still conscious, Kajin was the one who had brought me out. He didn't beat me, but he was standing on a curb or somewhere, four or five or six metres in the direction of number 3 and number 1. And for the rest of the beating I did not see Mr. Kajin there, but when they started beating me, he was around, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. At some point after this beating continued, did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I was already -- when you receive five or six such blows, I was -- I was kind of falling down, getting up. One gets up instinctively. And then again there were blows. I would fall. I don't know how long it went on. Approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know, 10, 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, just listen to my question. At some point during this beating, did you lose consciousness? That's a straight question.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you next became aware of something, in other words, when you awoke from this state of unconsciousness, what was the next thing you can recall?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Next, a metal barrel, there was water in it. I think it was a metal barrel with water from that metal barrel, and I held on with my hands. I held onto something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where was your head in relation to the water in the barrel?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess in the water before I came to. I was wet, so water, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How or what did you feel, other than being wet?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I felt -- no, I didn't feel any pain, I felt some kind of pressure here. I could not breathe. Then I -- then I felt strong pain on this side. I still react to changes to weather, very acute pain, I don't know how to put it, very sharp pain. I couldn't breathe properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And for the record, Witness, you are taking your hand and demonstrating for the Court your right side of your chest as you're giving your evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I apologise, yes. The right -- no, no, no, left -- of my left side, on the left side of my chest, more to the left and towards the head. I could not breathe. And I felt a very sharp pain, a truly sharp pain did I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Blows again on the legs, loins, I suppose, that is, the crotch. That is from the knees to the other side. My back, my head, then I fell. And then I felt -- but I was somewhere between unconsciousness and sort of semi -- half consciousness. But then I felt grass, which should mean that I wasn't on the asphalt, on the concrete, which meant that I was on the grass because I felt that grass. Then I felt the blows to the left side of my head, one, two, three, all over the body, and then I fainted again. I mean -- because at that time, it had already become batons or police truncheons. It wasn't rifle butts any more, or perhaps one used the baton and another one used a rifle butt, I can't say, because at that time I was already only semiconscious, and then I fainted completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. When you woke up from this second bout of unconsciousness, where did you find yourself?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I found myself in a small and dark room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you later find out where this room was located?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was number 1, the first one next to number 2, the small room. Next to it was the lavatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you referring to the lavatory or are you referring to a different room when you woke up?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, not lavatory. It's a small narrow space. I had not been there before or after, but it is a small and narrow space. How do I know that it was narrow? Because from where I was lying, I could see guards, seven, eight, ten guards or soldiers, I don't know who that was, but they were very near me. They were very near me, that is, when I woke up. There were guards, and in front of me were the two Banovics, right in front of me. And it's very narrow space. To the right, I recognise -- no, I didn't recognise it because it was dark, but they had their torches, their flashlights, a tall, younger man. And behind the back in right-hand corner, there was a man whom I did not know before, tall. At that time, I could not -- I could not really say what kind of clothes he had, but later on I realised what clothes he had. That is -- and I don't know if I told you, towards the back wall, there was a young man, short, thin, facing the wall. I could not see his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Apart from these guards that were there with flashlights or torches, as you call them, were there any other detainees in that room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That gentleman facing the wall was a prisoner, and the one to the right of me about half a metre away, maybe, he was also a prisoner. And I suppose while I was unconscious, I don't know how long that lasted, he must have been -- not must have been, he was beaten. During that time, he was beaten. I found that out later because he lay in number 1 across me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, would you just concentrate on the questions that you are asked and try to answer them to the best of your ability and as simply and as shortly as possible. The question was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 fairly simple, that is: Were there any other detainees in the room?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that your answer was yes to that. Did you know the name of any of the other detainees that were in that small little room with you when you woke up?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Detainees, no. But I heard from Banovic, I heard Banovics call him Tarzan. "Are you Tarzan? Are you that Tarzan?" A nickname or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My apologies. I said name, I also should have included nickname. Did you hear or did you know someone by the nickname of Tarzan to be in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Guards, guards called him Tarzan, guards, Banovics specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were the Banovics in that room with you and Tarzan?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened to you in relation to the Banovics and Tarzan, if anything?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. At that moment, I didn't know. I found out later, some 10, 15 days later that he had also been beaten that night and brought to the same room where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. While you were in the room and while Tarzan was in the room, did something happen to you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the Banovics, I don't know which one, took off my sweatsuit, forced me to stand up. And I was semiconscious, I was down on the floor. There was a wheelbarrow there, and I leaned, I supported myself against it and somehow managed to stand up. And they got me -- the trousers of my sweatsuit down, and then Tarzan had to kneel down - he was beaten all the time during that on the head and his back. And I apologise to all the listeners here, they got hold of my penis and put it in his mouth and beat him then. And I felt the pain down there, around the testicles and that part, because it was a police baton which was responsible for it. Very degrading, very mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: During the course of this incident, did you receive a burn to your hand or your arm?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: One of them got a lighter, a gas lighter, and started for my testicles. And I was about to put my hands down, and I apologise again, he scorched my pubic hair only, but then he burnt my hand, and I have it here. So that, fortunately, as far as those organs down there, I got off relatively lightly. But it was very hard for me, perhaps more than any other beatings, that humiliating, the degrading thing, very hard. I still have problems with that. I still smart from it psychologically, the situation that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Before yesterday, had you told anyone about that incident that you've just related to us?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: My wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, after that incident involving the lighter, what happened to you next while in that room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: And then that gentleman who stood to my right, I gleaned him somehow, a big, tall man, it was his turn then, and together with Banovics, he beat me, but I wasn't really aware of that. I don't know how long it took. But I felt, for instance -- yes, I did feel the difference between the military batons and the cable; that is, I found out later on that it was a power cable, and I saw it -- well, afterwards -- or at least pieces like that one, because that is a completely different type of blow. And I think it was then that they broke my ribs, the two ribs here, these here, and I think that was it. And I learnt later on that it was Mr. Duca. I didn't know his name then. That was really torturing, really, and I suppose it was then that the knife, or perhaps something else -- but in Zagreb the doctors told me that it was a knife. I have a cut here like this, and I have another cut down there, and I was also stabbed in the left shin. You can still see the scars. What was it? Of course, it got infected, and I mean -- but I do not know what that was, because I was not conscious when that happened, and I have no idea with what they did it, even though those cuts up here, down there, and above my knee and the one beneath the ribs the doctor told me that it was a knife. But down on my left leg, above the -- on the shin, above the -- above my foot, he could not say what that had been done with. But it was all on my left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that after this protracted series of beatings that you've just related to us, that you lost consciousness again?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Tarzan told me later on. I didn't know that they had beaten me, because that -- I fainted and I regained consciousness in Room 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just a moment, Witness. I just want to back you up to the point when you were still in the little room, the little dark room with Tarzan, and you've told us about an additional beating. Did you lose consciousness in that room again?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you recall being back at the water barrel at any point?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, outside. I came to over the water barrel. That is when I came to. Well, not quite. I didn't regain my consciousness fully, but I was sort of aware of my surroundings, halfway through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just stop there. Just stop there. When you became semi-aware of your surroundings, did you hear anyone say anything within your hearing?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I suppose when they got my head out of the water, so you -- just for a moment you are conscious. And I saw that Duca - that is, later on I found that it was Duca - he stood behind the barrel, and Banovics were behind me. That is, the barrel was right in front of me, Mr. Duca to the right. And what I heard was more or less - and I believe I already said that - he said something like -- of course, he cursed at my mother and he said, "This Turk is still alive," but in the Bosnian sense of the word, not -- how you translate it, how you have it in your statement. That is, he first cursed at my mother and then he said, "Now we'll see. Now you'll see," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I understand, sir, that you were beaten again and lost consciousness again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you woke up from this final bout of unconsciousness, where did you find yourself?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I found myself in the middle of Room 1, underneath a window or something, on the concrete, next to Mr. Namik. There was one Edhem Susic, a man of about 90, and between their legs -- no, not between, because they had their legs on me when I first came to on the concrete, down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't concrete. No. I think it was tiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir -- Witness, it really doesn't matter that much exactly where you were in the room or whether it was tiles or concrete. There are more significant things you can tell this Court. What I'm interested in: When you woke up, you were in Room 1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you find out from the other detainees how long you had been unconscious when you awoke in Room 1?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Afterwards -- well, according to what they told me, it was three or four days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: After you woke up in Room 1 after this prolonged period of unconsciousness, were you able to function normally?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. I don't understand what "normal functioning" means. I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you able to get up, move around, go to the bathroom, eat, sleep, drink?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What limitations were there on your activities?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: After that, when I woke up, I spent another ten days in a semiconscious state. I could see, I couldn't see; I'd faint, then come back to; hear people, not hear people; see, not see. And I felt horrible. A stench. I must have defecated. And blood too, I suppose. Horrible stench.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, how did you get food or water? Could you eat?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did other prisoners help you with respect to getting you some water from time to time? Sorry. I didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I couldn't take in food or water at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, after that last incident, were you beaten again while you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, do I understand correctly, sir, that this beating happened almost the first day that you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The first hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sorry. I understand that within the day there was -- this beating happened almost immediately upon your arrival at Keraterm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Naturally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And after the incidents that you've described to us in some detail, you were not beaten again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, about ten days before the camp closed, did something happen with respect to -- were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: About 10, maybe 15 -- no, 10, 12 days, yes, they interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was just 10 days before the camp closed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Ten to twelve days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember how it was that you came to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I was called out from a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know how that list was created?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't, but I suppose that when detainees arrived, they made lists and then followed a sequence, or rather -- I don't know how they made those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You were interrogated, sir. I understand that was a relatively -- they just asked you normal questions and you were taken back to Room 1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were at Keraterm camp, did you have occasion to see --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. May I add something very important for me, for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Ranko Bucalo, whom I knew pretty well and who was my interrogator. There was another gentleman in a uniform and trainers. Him, I didn't know. And so I said, "What am I doing here?" That is, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 wanted to find out: Was he -- did he realise what he was doing? And I got no answer. This is of vital importance for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will ask you to listen carefully to the questions that counsel is asking because he has a special reason for asking them, and just answer those questions as precisely as possible. Continue, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but it is very important for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we appreciate that, yes.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It needs to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, while you were at Keraterm camp, I understand there was an occasion when you saw some dead bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances under which you saw those dead bodies and when and where that was.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In the morning, before 5.00, before the shift change. I had gone to drink some water, but I would not keep anything, water or food, dysentery or something. And when I could, I urinated in a bottle, but I couldn't do that even. So I asked the guards to come out earlier, and one of them was a pupil of mine. And that morning, he let me out, going beyond the rules which were there, that is, the guards did not let prisoners to the lavatory before 5.00, but they let me out. And I came out, and I could -- to the right of me, there was some garbage or something, and I remember seeing there three men. After that day -- and, sir, I did not explain it to you proper when we discussed. After that, there were more people that day, I don't remember the date, in some inspection of sorts came, from the police or somebody because a number of people had been killed. We did not come out at that time. There were five, six, seven dead men. Mr. Sikirica also came. I do not know him yet, but it was from the stories that I heard. I don't know and I'm not interested. But we did not come out, and it was when those men were picked up -- well, it was that morning that I went to the lavatory, and it could not last more than four or five minutes, and it was then that I saw those men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And those men that you saw, could you tell if they were dead or alive?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: What shall I tell you? I think they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to turn your mind now to an occasion in mid-July when you and your other detainees were lined up for lunch. Did an incident occur while you were in the lunch lineup that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you do that now, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, in short, we were standing in the line. There was a guard, he was toothless. I don't know which one it was. He was sitting in a chair. And then we had to start going when he knocked with the rifle butt. Along with me, there was a cleric, a hodza or imam.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, a hodza, or imam, is a Muslim priest or Muslim clergyman?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, a cleric. He received a lot of beating there with rifle butts, batons. There were several guards involved. He would get up, fall down. It was -- he was an older man with a heart condition. I think he had suffered two heart attacks. I knew him fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you tell whose shift was on at the time this beating of the Muslim hodza took place?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kole. He was there. He was some distance away, maybe five, six metres away, but he did not beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would he have been able to see this beating from where he was?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This Kole, do you know who -- what position Kole had in the camp?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He was guard commander, a commander or chief of the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, later, when I started going out, he would come. I was once with him in the toilet, and I was feeling ill. They brought me to the toilet, that is something -- we were in a hurry. I was sitting on a crate. I was feeling sick. It was, I think, a plastic crate for beer or sodas in the front part of the toilet and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, the size or the construction of the crate isn't really that significant to my question. How did you know Kole? Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: This is where I met him in person, that is, number one. In number two I saw bars, movements, lunch, how shall I put it? This went on my -- for about 15 days, I was able to move about freely, that is, sometimes during his shift, we were able to come out -- during his shift, food was also brought in, but my wife, who was an ethnic Serb, could not pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right. And your answer to my question as to how you knew him is then that you saw him during these days that you were able to walk around; is that it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how frequently would you see this individual that you've referred to as Kole?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: We knew the shifts. I knew, for instance, that he was in the shift with the Banovics, with Mr. Milan. That was a young, tall man, almost 2 metres tall, whom I had known from before. He walked around in their company, then specifically I saw him. I had met my -- with my wife, and Milan mediated, and I also had some cigarettes which I had gotten and I shared some with them, and Banovics were also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My question is not in relation to Milan at the moment. I'm asking you how you know Kole. Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So your exposure to Kole was restricted to what you saw at Keraterm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you obtain information -- just listen to my question before you answer -- did you obtain information from the other detainees concerning Kole as to who he was or what his position was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, one could see this, not by inmates only. He was ordering this, ordering that. It is immediately clear who is number one by a series of actions when the lunch was distributed. But all inmates knew who was who. And in those 15 days, there was a number of opportunities for me to learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, I'll come back to Kole in a moment, but I just want to deal now with early -- well, not early July, but a few days before the 24th or 25th of July. Are you aware, to your personal knowledge, that new prisoners were arriving from the Carakovo area?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How did you see that they were arriving? Like, how could you see?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I saw a group of people. How else is one to say? There were a lot of them. I first saw beating at the scales. We called that area "scales." That is the area where I had been searched. It was intense beating, a mass beating. There were a lot of people, many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You've told us what you saw. Now I'm going to ask my original question, which is: What was your vantage point; how were you able to see? Were you in the open? Were you in the room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In the room. No, we were in the room. We were locked up. We could not go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there some unique construction about the doors in Room 1 where you were an inmate that allowed you to see out?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The door and that hall opening was covered with metal bars, I think maybe 7, 8 millimetres thick, spaced 10 to 15 centimetres. So through that opening, you could see out, of course, as much as the width of the opening allowed, depending on what you looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from Room 1 and from these open spaces in the bars, did you have a clear vantage point of the reception area near the weigh scales of Keraterm camp where these people arrived?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the best vantage point from number 1 to see straight out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, you've told us, sir, that you saw beating going on, and did these prisoners arrive all in one group or in several groups, or can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: From what I could see, I think they arrived in two groups. I think that it was on the same day. They did not go into the rooms immediately. They were not assigned to them as the others -- as the inmates -- they were on this pista. This is this concrete, paved area in the middle. They were beaten, constantly beaten, and they would be threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you understand my question? Who beat the new arrivals on this occasion that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The guards. It was the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was it only guards that beat these new prisoners or were any people from your room involved somehow?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two young men, maybe 18, 19 years old. They were singing those -- these Chetnik songs along with them. At one point, I don't know if they were forced or not, one of these two was blond, and the other one was even younger. They were forced. They said, "We had to."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Had to what?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: To beat them. They were at the pista a bit to the left, and there was a group of people in a circle and we were -- watching this. All the prisoners saw this. And those two men came out and -- they were hit, blows on the head, back. Those men were sitting down. They were not standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: From what you could see, apart from the beatings, were these new prisoners fed or given water?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The first days when -- I don't know if there were any men in Room 4, but in Room 3, no. I don't know whether there was three -- two, three, four days, but during the first days, no, because we knew when the food arrived. Towards the end, it was 4.00 or 5.00 in the evening. They weren't there when the food was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. My question now is: Do you know where these new prisoners were placed ultimately, eventually?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In number 3. A large number in number 3. Maybe there were some others placed elsewhere, but most of them in number 3. And I know because there had been some men in number 3 before they arrived and then they moved them, because part of these men was also moved to our room, number 1, and perhaps even to Room 2. I'm not sure of that. But there were men who had come from Room 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Men had come from Room 3 and had been placed in your room, and then ultimately these new arrivals, I understand from your evidence, sir, were placed in Room 3; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, do you recall an evening that you would refer to when you heard a lot of shooting?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you tell us about -- I'm now directing your attention to that evening, if that's clear. Can you tell us what happened that night, leading up to and during the shooting.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: First we heard -- in fact, every vehicle that would come to Keraterm we would recognise. We would recognise it by its engine. And on that occasion an extraordinarily large number of vehicles arrived, and that was kind of like a sixth sense, a sense that some danger was coming. There were headlights, and these headlights lit the entire area, the entire area of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Apart from your sixth sense and noticing these additional lights lighting up the area, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some commotion. I was part of the reserve force, and I heard the sound which to me sounded like a German-made machine-gun, M-50 something, and then there was also like a rattle of automatic weapons and then shouts and footsteps running around. This is all before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us about the incident when there was further shooting? About what time of day was that, or night?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That was not in daylight. At around 9.00 we had to -- how shall I say? We had to get quiet. So maybe an hour, an hour and a half had elapsed, but we didn't have watches. It wasn't easy to place it in time, and to me it wasn't that important anyway, to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right. So moving on to what is important, can you tell us what you heard, sir?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Shooting. First it was individual shots, individual shots, perhaps even pistol shots, then bursts of fire, smashing of -- breaking of glass. This is what we heard initially. Screams. A horror to us. This is how we felt. People screaming. It was terrible. Noise. But the dominant noise was the automatic weapon fire, and it seemed to us as an eternity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you able to put an approximation of what eternity actually probably was in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe that most intense shooting, the bursts with the most rounds fired, perhaps 20, 25 minutes. It is very hard for me to say. After that, there were individual shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to ask you: Do you know whose shift was on duty the night of what I'm now going to refer to as "the massacre"?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kole's.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Because I saw him that day. I saw the guards who were part of that shift. I'm sure that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what time of the day the shifts changed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In the morning, I think -- I think the shift changed around 5.00 in the morning. This is what we were interested in. Depending on the commander of the guard, we were allowed or not allowed to go to the toilet. That was as far as Room 1 is concerned, not Room 2. They could -- Room 2 could go at 3.00 or something. I'm only referring to Room 1. When you passed 5.00 in the morning, that is apparently when the shift was changing, and we would be let out, three, four at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, sir, just one moment. What I'm trying to establish is the times of the shift change. Now, you say that in the morning they would change at 5.00, or thereabouts, in regard to Room 1. Was there a further shift change later in the day or would there only be one shift change per day?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I think that a shift lasted 12 hours. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Now, sir, this Kole that you've referred to, is that the same individual that you say you saw earlier in the camp when you referred to the beating of the Muslim priest?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you feel, sir, that from your seeing this individual you referred to as Kole in the camp, that you would be able to recognise him in the event that you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, ten years, things change. I assume he was -- he had his hair longer. It was longer then. He was wearing a military uniform, a pistol on the right-hand side, a police baton on the left-hand side. He was fairly thin then. At the toilet I took a good look at him, and to me he was okay. He didn't beat me. He even let me stay on that crate in the toilet. He did not hit me. I explained to him that I couldn't go, and everybody else had to go in, and he let me stay on that crate in that urine and, with your apologies, in that shit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand that. You may have lost sight of my question. In the event that you were to see this man again, do you feel that you would be able to recognise him from your association with him in Keraterm some nine years ago? Would you recognise him again if you were to see him?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I assume that it is that gentleman over there. That is, he changed quite a bit, and I did. He is between two police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in the previous testimony there was no evidence on how the witness has learned the name of the person that he is attempting to identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But let the witness conclude the answer he was giving, and then, Mr. Ryneveld, we'll determine what he wants to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All I really want to find out from the witness is if he thinks he would recognise him. If he can, let him say so; if he can't, let him say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already purported to identify one of them. He said it was between the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you pointing to the back wall, sir, over there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There are, by my estimate --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Between the two police officers. I think that's the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Counting from right to left, what seat --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: From right to left, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what seat is he occupying?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: From right to left, in the second seat, between two police officers, according to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All right, sir. Now, the following morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, would you stop for a while. Mr. Ryneveld, the Chamber is consulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, will you say, for the record, who was identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, it appears that, for the record, the witness has identified Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
