utterances.text: Now, sir, the following day, were you allowed out of your room after this shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you saw the loading of bodies onto a truck and then the truck left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it also fair to say --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I saw a truck with a canopy. I think it was a civilian truck. I say that because of the canopy. And we saw this. We were facing the wall, that is, that means that we were facing the other way, all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, just bear with me for a moment. What I'm trying to do is get the effect of your evidence, sir. I understand that you saw a truck arrive, you saw it with a canopy, and it left. Is it fair to say that you later heard that bodies were placed in that truck; is that correct? You heard from the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you want directly, that man next to me had a small mirror with plastic frame, very thin, four or five millimetres thin. And I warned him because of the reflection of the sun, so he was angling it so we could see what was going on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, stop the witness when you think you've had enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I've tried but, unfortunately, I didn't get an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He remains your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Although that may be a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, some parts of your evidence, you understand, is more significant than others, and if I am wrong, please correct me, but when I suggest something to you and it's correct, we don't necessarily need every detail. I understand that, through a mirror, you were able to see a truck arriving and leaving, and you heard from other prisoners that bodies were loaded onto that truck; is that correct? Am I wrong about that? You are nodding your head, meaning yes, I'm right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, you're not wrong, but the case with the mirror was a moment after it was done, and the story about when and what, that is -- that is something else. But if you want to know what I saw with my own eyes was a wheel, a tyre that was covered in blood. And this I could see from where I was. So that is how much blood there was that I could see that, and it was also on the canopy, if that is what you're after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. If I was, I would have asked you, sir. Now, I understand, sir, that a couple of days after this incident, you were one of the first people to be allowed out of your room in order to go to the toilet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I take it from that that you had not been permitted to leave the room for some period of time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you did go to the toilet, did you see into Room 3?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Room 3, no, I did not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry, the toilet. What can you tell us about the condition of the toilet, which I understand is next to Room 3; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In addition to urine and faeces, blood, and a mirror that was across from the door, I would check myself to see how I looked. I saw blood, but they did not wash it properly. I saw that there was pieces of hair. I had about five, six minutes. I tried to throw up, but there was nothing to throw up. I felt nausea. I felt sickness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is the time for the break. It would be useful Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 if we could conclude the examination-in-chief, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would like to, but do you want me to do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: After the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, we are going to adjourn now and return at half past 2.00. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, will you complete the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just before the lunch break, I was about to ask you, sir, I understand that you were in Keraterm until the 3rd of August when you were put on some buses and taken to Trnopolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphones for the witness are switched off.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, a short period of time before you were taken away, sir, were another group taken away separately?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I can say a day before I was taken away, one day before, one of the guards allowed me, probably with the authorisation of the chief of the guards, allowed me to see -- to meet my wife. And as a matter of fact, that is the only guard whom I really know. Those other men, I do not know, hence the confusion. The changes are on a major scale. So my wife brought me some food, two packages of cigarettes, and some medicines, and a change of underwear. And that guard took me to the ramp, to the entrance behind the scales.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the witness said, "Hence, the confusion," and I presume he meant the identification, but this is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can this be verified? I think, perhaps, Mr. Ryneveld, if you could get the witness just to repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript shows "confusion." I think that my learned friend is asking the assumption behind that, but the witness, I don't think, said it, but maybe he did. I will ask the question, although it's not really in response to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, when you say, "Those other men I do not know, hence the confusion," what confusion are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I meant the confusion regarding Mr. Kajin, meaning Mr. -- what's his name -- Kole. I was in a rather poor shape. Now, people whom I see here, a major change has occurred. I've changed too. But with Mr. Kole, I was tete-a-tete in the lavatory, and what I told you is all true. At that time, he looked to me slightly different. But he stood next to me. I know he was not as tall, and I know he was relatively fair with somewhat longish hair, military uniform, a pistol in one hand, baton on the other, army boots. And those men here, I recognise the eyes of the gentlemen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, because counsel is on his feet, making an objection.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The procedure of identification has already been carried out by the Prosecutor, and the record reflects who was the person identified by this witness. The witness has already testified about identification, about personal characteristic of that witness, and now after a break and after him, you know, reflecting what he might have said, and the colloquy which occurred between Mr. Petrovic and the counsel, I believe this would not be a proper form to identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think any identification is being made now, Mr. Vucicevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was, as a matter of fact, at the invitation of the Court, at my friend's suggestion, that I attempted to clarify what he meant by "confusion." I think it's now clear that he was talking about the confusion about an earlier attempt at identification. I want to leave that, if I may. Unless my friend, Mr. Petrovic, wants to cross-examine later, I propose to move on to my original question, which was, sir:

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think you've told us that a guard whom you knew took you to the gate to allow you to receive a package of some items brought to you by your wife. Can you tell us the identity of that guard?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that. I know him. I know him very well indeed. I've known him for a long time, because I was his teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And his name is?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: May I not say his name? If I have to, I will, but I'd rather not, because he might suffer some consequences of that. But if you -- if I must, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In any event --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid he might have some problems. Well, then, his name is Milan --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you his name. On the basis of your explanation, I take it this is a Serb gentleman?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And he was a pupil of yours?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, you got this package from your wife, and did you have any conversation with this guard concerning something that happened later?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: We talked right away, there, at the ramp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: And he told me that the list of men who were - at least, that is how I gathered - which was on the investigator's desk, that is, upstairs, as you go up the stairs and into the room where we were interrogated, that there was a list. At that time, I didn't really understand what this was, and that my name was not on that list. And I had somewhat mixed feelings about it, but as I was returning, I began to be rather anxious about that list, afraid. I began to think about it, I mean subconsciously. That is, I wasn't happy to think that there was a list, because the knowledge that there was a list somehow rang the bell; that is, I thought of those other lists, calling out men, their disappearance, young men being taken out to work and never coming back. That was the association that I had when this list of men was mentioned, and I felt rather ill at ease.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So you were told there was a list, you were concerned about the fact that a list existed, but you were told your name was not on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The following day -- what can you tell us what happened the following day in relation to the list?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: There were many policemen arrived, in cars, in vehicles, in buses. We saw that the situation was not an everyday situation, not as before that. Before that, I must say, we cleaned the rooms. We were even allowed to bathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you? Perhaps I didn't state my question clearly. The following day --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes. You were quite clear, but I want to describe the situation as it was then, because it was of major importance for me and those who were inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question that counsel asks. He knows why he's asking the question. And don't offer any further explanations or any further descriptions unless the Court requires it of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you wanted to tell us that preparations were made to clean the room and to leave the camp, but in the course of that, at some point did you count something? Did something happen that made you personally count something? And if so, what happened? Tell us about that incident. That's what I'm directing your mind to now, please.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, that morning, that morning, around 8.00 or 9.00, thereabouts, so these buses and cars arrived, and so on and so forth, and they began to call men out from a list. And since I knew that I wasn't on the list, and with that feeling, with that anxiety and all the rest, when they started to call out -- and it was somebody outside who was calling out people outside Room 1, or perhaps a bit further away - I don't know who that was - but men were called out from that list. Men were called out. And when all the men had been called out, they boarded a bus and they were the first ones to leave Keraterm. Naturally, the place was teeming with police, with troops. Then to our room, and I'm now talking about Room 1, an officer entered - I think he was Captain First Class, whom I do not know - and roughly, roughly said the following: "The rest of you are innocent. You're free, and you'll go to Trnopolje."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. When the list of names was read out, did you personally keep count?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I counted, I believe other people kept count too, but knowing that I was not on the list I suppose I was in such a state of mind so that I counted 126 people, I think that is the exact figure, even though, according to your papers, it's 129. But I counted 126 men, including ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, after this man said the rest of you are innocent, you're free Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 to go, we're taking you to Trnopolje, or words to that effect, were you, in fact, loaded on buses and taken to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, after a while, but, yes, we boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The bottom line is that you got on buses, you were taken to Trnopolje, and you stayed at Trnopolje until the 13th of August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: A couple more very basic questions, sir. How heavy were you when you were taken prisoner on the 23rd of June and taken to Keraterm? What was your body weight?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: 109, 110 kilograms, something about that, 109, 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was your body weight when you were released?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, about 66, 67, and as my wife cleaned me, she said, Now you've lost another kilogram.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that because of the absence of food at the camp?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. In the beginning, in the beginning, I could not eat. I could not drink or -- could not either drink or eat because I was all swollen, my teeth and everything, and I was all black. I had wounds on my body and even worms, worms began to appear, some dark and then some white and long, and then a doctor who was next to me, he said if it's white worms your organism will manage to fend off, but for about 15 days, I only drank water as much as I could for about 15 or 16 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Would you answer my learned friends, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, is this your first time here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I imagine you are looking forward to going home, are you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, you can help me and you can help yourself to get home quicker and we're going to do a deal about the questions I'm going to ask you; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I shall be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The deal is this, Mr. Hidic: I'm going to ask you, for about 20, 25 minutes some questions. Listen carefully to what I ask you and answer the question and then you'll get home that much quicker. Is that a fair deal?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Right. Let's see how we get on. The school at which you were a teacher, is this correct that it functioned effectively right up until the end of May 1992, just before the serious trouble started? Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I apologise. How do you mean "worked"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the sense that you and your colleagues kept on going to work, the students kept on coming, I have no doubt the tensions were rising, but as far as possible, you tried to maintain a normal existence for yourself, your colleagues, and the students; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the course of that month of May 1992, were there meetings which were taking place amongst the staff and discussions as to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. That is, at that time, there was a meeting of the faculty of the teachers together with the school council, which is a kind of a steering board, and the principal -- and the principal, the former principal. There was a change and another man was appointed. I was present at the meeting, but I didn't attend other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us about this: The staff was, I think, something in the region of 130 teachers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, with auxiliary staff. I wouldn't know exactly, but with the auxiliary staff, it should be, yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it right that the staff were drawn from all the ethnic backgrounds that existed in the Prijedor district?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Except the Romany, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that included Muslims, Croats and I think Ukranians and there is a Ukrainian population in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: And Serbs. And Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That is, first came Muslims, then Serbs, then Croats, Ukranians -- well, it's difficult for those who are in that area. One knows who is Catholic, who is not. Well, those people know, so it was here or there, but there are Ukranians by origin and what their option was, and who they said they were, that is their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would this be correct that, of those teachers, about 30 per cent were Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: We didn't count, but that is roughly the -- their share. You must understand that until 1989, until 1989, that is practically until Gazimestan, that is when the situation in our area began to get complicated. Those in that area, they know, then began altercations. We simply did not count. How shall I put it? If you have a school, if you work in a school -- I worked in Omarska; I mean, those children were the same to me as those in Kozarac because I did the same kind of work, the same kind of effort, and that pupil invested a great deal of effort to also learn something, to be trained, because they were learning some mechanical trades or some technical trades, and it really wasn't that important. It wasn't in the foreground. But I think that, yes, the share was roughly that one, but we never counted one another. There was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I turn now, please, to your arrival at Keraterm camp, Mr. Hidic. Two things: You weren't beaten and you weren't interrogated at that time. You weren't interrogated immediately upon your arrival.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Would you be specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course. Upon your arrival at Keraterm camp, you were not, at that time, interrogated; you were interrogated after you'd been there for some time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Amongst those who were obviously the officials and authorities in the camp, were you able to observe that there were a large number of different uniforms being worn by those people?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, there were parts of -- some would wear, for instance -- Mr. Kajin, whom I remember such as I knew him at that time, he, for instance, had a red cap, a beret, a short undershirt, military trousers, and I believe trainers. Mr. Kole, whom I remember, had a military uniform, one summer uniform, boots, pistol on the one hand, truncheon on the other, and I don't remember these things about Mr. Kajin. That is true. Other soldiers, for instance this pupil of mine, he, for instance, wore a military uniform. Now, there were some soldiers, say -- well, that is not that I was accustomed to in the army which I respected for 20 years. I was in its reserve and -- so I hope I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, just answer the question directly and, Mr. Greaves, I would urge you to stop the witness when you have had your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I don't like to intervene, because in the last trial I did, I was accused of harassing witnesses when I tried to cut them short, so I'm a bit sensitive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, you've just been talking about your service in the JNA. Did you get the -- when you were in the JNA, what sort of unit were you in? Infantry, artillery, what?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Artillery. Artillery. I spent three months in Vranje, six months I attended a course in Strumica, and then from Strumica, which is in Macedonia, next to the Bulgarian border, between Bulgaria and Macedonia, and from there, I went back to Vranje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, it's fascinating, but I don't need your life history, all right? What I do want to ask you is --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: This is what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Just take it easy. When you were in the JNA, I have no doubt the JNA was a well-organised, well-disciplined force, is that fair, and you were proud to be a part of your artillery unit? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: This is a comprehensive question and I don't think I have time to respond to it now, because you have to have some patience if you want the real answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please. It was a straightforward question. Mr. Greaves, don't bother with this sort of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to get one point, and if you'll just -- just bear with me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's get on; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By comparison with when you were in the army, the people who were in all these different uniforms in the camp, did you have the impression that they were nowhere near as organised and smart as you had been when you were in the artillery in the JNA, Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: For what they were involved in, that is, their jobs, they were, because I would not have engaged in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you, as you watched them doing their jobs, unimpressed with the way in which they were organised, unimpressed with the way in which they were dressed? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: For me, this is a tangential question, but let me answer it anyway. No. I don't know why you're asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question. Never mind why he's asking it. If he's not to ask it, we will make that determination. Please give an answer as simply as possible.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Will you please ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, when you were interrogated later on, you knew who the people who were interrogating you were. Was it just one person or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Just one person. Two persons were present and one interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was it the person that you knew who was asking the questions?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew each other, relatively speaking, by sight and through family. Let's say it was sort of a wider circle of acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did the questions involve whether you had been involved in politics, whether you had been involved in military activity, whether you knew of the activities of extremists and things like that? Would that be a fair summary of what you were asked? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He asked me whether I had weapons, whether I was a member of the SDA, where were you, who is your neighbour, what did you do while you were in the house, do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The answer, in fact, is yes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I haven't finished. I haven't finished. Did I know Medunjanin, did I know this so-and-so. I was not a local. I was born in another town. I knew a lot of people by sight, those who were around town, that is. So it was long questioning, 45 minutes. That was a long questioning compared to the others, because he asked me to explain certain things. For instance, he asked me whether I was pro-Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Greaves, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, it's right, isn't it, that you were not beaten during the course of this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was it a guard who collected you and took you to the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: The guard was a young soldier, fair-haired, tall, good-looking, with a rifle. He brought me and then he took me back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is that the only part that he played in that exercise?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He brought me in and brought me back; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, my attention has been drawn to the transcript. I heard the answer to the question as to whether he was beaten or not during the course of the interrogation that he indicated that he had not been, and I hope that's my learned friend's recollection. The answer has come up to my question as a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What part of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you look at 15:04:28 and the answer thereto, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can this be verified? Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The difficulty is the way I think the question is phrased with a "not" in there, when the witness says "no" to a "not." My understanding is the witness was not beaten during the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not follow the thing very well. I was only beaten one night, and after that, I was not even touched. I stated that even before, and I know what you have in front of you. So I was not beaten any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the issue of who was in command of the camp. You were told who the camp commander was; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They mentioned Sikirica, but I never knew the man. Some people said that he had died. No. I heard that while I was in the apartment, that that person who was there had died. And then when I came to the camp after I don't know how much time, I learned that some person named Sikirica was the camp commander. I even now do not know, and I never saw him, and I don't see quite well. I would need glasses, eyeglasses. But I did not know him and I didn't see him on the pista, and in the condition that I was in, the condition of my health, I was not in a position to identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question you were asked was whether you were told who the camp commander was.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. We have that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what you told the Prosecutor in 1998 was that you couldn't remember his name but that you thought he had died of a heart attack. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That is a part. This is an excerpt. This is a part of my statement. It is a part of my statement, and it's not relevant for the Tribunal, but I know who died and who the person was who died. But we are not going to go into that. But in the camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, was the man who died called Zivko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is that someone who you had heard of before the war?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: As far as Zivko Knezevic is concerned, I kind of knew him by sight. I think that he had worked for the police. He was an older man, maybe 60 years old. I don't know exactly. He was frequently to be seen on the corso, the main drag. This is as much as I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hidic, shortly before your release from Keraterm, or shortly before leaving Keraterm, it's correct that the Serbs released all those people who they had managed to detain who were older than 60 or younger than 15. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the day when everybody departed from Keraterm. You've spoken about a Captain First Class who you saw during the course of that day. It's right, isn't it, that he also was the one who read out the list of names of those who were to go to Omarska? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, and that is not how it's stated. That's not what you have. He just entered Room 1 and he had said what I have said he said. And the reading out of the 126 names, we all had to get. That took place somewhere in the area between Rooms 1 and 2. I don't know who it was who was reading out those names and I never saw this person. I was somewhere in the middle, somewhere in the area where I was sleeping. And this Captain First Class just said, "You are now free. You are going to be going to Trnopolje." And I think that that is what you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remember talking to a gentleman called Ross in September of last year, Mr. Hidic, Ross Arden?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remember telling him and signing a statement in which you said, "On the morning of the 3rd of August an army Captain First Class called out 126 names of prisoners. I do not know his name. These prisoners were put on buses and left the camp." Do you remember telling him that and signing a statement to that effect?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I remember. I signed it and I remember it, but that's not how it was, because later on, I reconsidered it, and I did sign it and I said that this is how it was, and the others will also corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If it wasn't right, why did you put it in the statement, Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Because the time was very short, the time of his questioning. His questioning was together with another questioning, and we were making excerpts and I think what you have, it's somewhere on page 5 or 6, there was some discrepancy in the interpretation and then transferring to the computer, and that's what happened by the time I got back the materials. But the facts are there, because that is it. I see no reason about those 126 people. I didn't need to. I did not need to say something else. But I think that there was some misunderstanding, some miscommunication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You did, of course, sign an acknowledgment at the end of the statement, saying that the statement had been read over to you in your language and that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that, yes. And I made corrections when I reviewed the documents and compared to my recollection. Now, more of that is coming up, and also eight years have gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Recollection not very good after eight years, nine years; is that part of the problem?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Some things, and I was being honest here; some things yes, but other things I will never forget. And some other things - how shall I put it? If you're going to rely on it, they're fading, because the human mind is trying to push aside. It is a defence of sorts. Some things are fading, and I personally only manage two hours of sleep a night. That is also true. Don't misunderstand me. I'm also saying this because of these people that are sitting over there, that they could learn something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just one final question, Mr. Hidic, and it's quite simple, so listen to it and answer it as quickly as you can. You also told Ross Arden in September of last year that you didn't know Sikirica and didn't know him as the camp commander. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Not in that way. I did not know him personally. I did not see him. That is the difference between -- this is how one has to distinguish about interpretation and - how shall I put it? It is natural that I would hear in the camp that Sikirica was the commander. Who was the chief of shift, this is what one learns. These are -- and it was in that sense that I said that I had not known him, and I don't think that I would have recognised him now, nor do I think that I would have known him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, the phrase, sentence, "I did not know Sikirica, I did not know him as the camp commander," that is quite a simple pair of sentences, isn't it, and I suggest extremely difficult to mistranslate something like that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but that is what I had in mind when I said, and this is what I had in mind before. And trust me, for anyone who had spent a couple of days there, that person knew, knew who was a shift commander, and those people who were born there, they know who was there, because there were peers, they were all born there. To me, all that -- perhaps it was not interpreted well, but one million per cent, that was it. And it all has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hidic.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I listened to you and I noticed a problem, that is, that you have a lot to say, and the time here is limited. So what we are trying to do is really to cull what is the most significant, both my friends from the Prosecution and on this side of the bench too, and I know that you can speak at length about what the subject is here today. When you were answering the Prosecutor's questions earlier, he asked you about the situation in 1992, what it was like. However, my question to you would be more specific: Can you clarify for us when did these divisions between ethnic groups in Bosnia start? Was that in 1992 or did it start somewhat earlier?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that you are aware that these are -- that you are casting your net wide. I don't know, the people around here may not be fully aware of this. As you know, the division started much earlier. In my case, the sense that I had was that as early as my army days, that's when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, let us not go that far back, and there are individual cases perhaps, but let's talk about the national-based or ethnic-based Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 parties. Was it at that time that these disruptions really took hold?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It started earlier. And I think that you are aware of them. Shall I explain it for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I think that we have an understanding, you and I, but it's a very long story.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that you did your national service in Vranje Strumica?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: And then back to Vranje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And it was the artillery?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I ended up as a lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that you spent quite a bit of time with the reserve force, some 20 years, exercises?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a reservist, and then five, six -- I was an instructor of the recruits for target practice for five or six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what was that unit, the reserve unit that you were in?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: That was the Banja Luka regiment. It was the Prijedor battalion. I had a fellow friend from Petrovac who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us about the discipline, and if you can make a comparison between the active-duty military and the reserve force. Was there a difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: You mean at the time when I served?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then later on when you were on the reserve force. Can we say that, as far as discipline was concerned, that it was more lax, shall we put it, in comparison to what it was when you served --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: You know what? I was the commanding officer for quite a while for my reserve battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I am just asking you in general.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: As far as general matters are concerned, when there was real target practice, and these exercises with preparations lasted for 10, 15 days, that was fairly disciplined, like in the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that you went to work until, I think, 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think it was 25th or 26th. It was a Friday, I believe, Friday or Monday. It can be calculated from the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Until then, were you able to go to work without problems?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but where are you from? You know my data, but I want to know yours. I am from Sarajevo. Last ten, 15 days, Mr. Rodic, you could already sense the takeover of the television relay on Mrakovica, the cutting off of the Sarajevo television and then patching it up to Banja Luka, and then of a sea change in programming on Radio Prijedor. If that is what you're referring to, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I was just thinking between home and work.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they were calling them, barriers or -- one was manned by Serbs, the other by us Bosniaks, and then the police was regrouping. One wanted this, the other one wanted that. I did not -- my field of interest was different. I wasn't going into that. I was more into sociology, music, sports, arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 23rd of June, you were arrested around 7.00 p.m., that your child notified you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. The child came up and then I went down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned a policeman named Strika?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that an active duty police officer?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: For a while he was active. I don't know at that point, but he -- he would stop me quite a few -- he stopped me quite a few times to check me and my vehicle. Even on the eve of war, whether I had a first aid kit, all that stuff, to see whether my vehicle was in good order. But for a good period of time, he was an active duty police officer and he was wearing this active duty police officer uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I need to follow the transcript.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you said 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You were able to follow the time by your watch?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You waited for two hours to be questioned, that is, for someone to talk to you and then Strika invited you -- called you into another room?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. Strika told me, "Sit down and wait." And then my wife arrived from the apartment and she joined me, and she was there with me until Strika took me. The first was the duty room, duty desk, and then there was -- next to it was a small room. He took my identity card, took down my name. I don't know if he took down any other information on the piece of paper, and then I sat down. So then we went to the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So two hours later, you left the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to you, after you overheard the conversation in the vehicle; Omarska, Keraterm, and then eventually you were taken to Keraterm, do you know who it was that decided that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Strika, because the other soldier was younger. He was junior, so Strika decided it. He also decided that in respect of Ms. Suada Ramic and she, indeed, spent the night at Keraterm. I don't know what happened to her afterwards. This is based on the other people's stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the person who met you at Keraterm --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- I'll say it and then you just tell me whether this is right or not. In the transcript, in the record, during the main examination, that is, you said in respect of this man as follows: "I am not sure that I would be able to recognise him now because I could still -- I would still not be able to recognise due to all the time that has passed."

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: And other circumstances, not knowing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, we are running into a technical problem if you keep interrupting me.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat this.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: My apologies again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So what you said was this: "I am not sure that I would be able to recognise him now because I still wouldn't be able to recognise him. I think that this was Mr. Kajin. I think that this is what he was called." Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: In that sense, no. That's not what I said. I said that Namik had asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'll come to that. This is just an introductory question.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then when the Prosecutor asked you, you described that man and said that he was short, I think about 186?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fat, short-sleeved T-shirt, military uniform, military uniform, about 176 centimetres tall, fat, wearing a red cap, rather rounded off face. Did not beat anyone at the entrance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Did not beat me. I wasn't beaten at the entrance. But the description had to do with his uniform rather than his -- that is at least how, in the semi-darkness, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is how you described it to the Prosecutor, and I'm only asking you to check it.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also, when asked by the Prosecutor, said that other prisoners were the ones who had told you that it was Kajin, more specifically, Mr. Namik, your friend whom you knew from before.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He asked me, yes, "What did Kajin ask you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you entered Room 1 and saw Mr. Namik there, can you tell me, in view of the size of the room, which part of it was Mr. Namik and --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: And you tell me I have no time for a broader explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No. There is no time, and we know the size of the room.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Right. Right. Right. I'll tell you clearly. About the middle of the room to the left, there's a radiator next to it, a narrow window which could be opened, a glass with metal frame. And Namik lay there, then Edhem Susic next to him, and then this sequence of sleeping was kept throughout. Then a man called Islamovic and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, when you entered, did you find him lying in that place?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He was crouching.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Crouching?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. And there was no room for me to sit down, I stood. I don't know if the gentlemen know what crouching means or squatting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: They do. And between Mr. Namik and the door, between Mr. Namik, that is, where he squatted and the entrance door, were there people there, and how many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, 100, 80, I didn't count them. I didn't know where I'd entered, but roughly, roughly give or take in that part. I'm completely at sea now, but I was taken aback to see that it was so packed, that there was no room for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean squatted, crouching, sitting?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, sitting, squatting, and that silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, during your stay in the camp at Keraterm, did you ever witness medical aid being extended to somebody or a physician coming to examine somebody during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Namik urged with somebody, because I was in a poor shape, that I should go to a doctor, that I should go somewhere. But -- and I don't know who said, "Just throw him out." At that time, I was unconscious and that is what Namik told me and Mr. Islamovic also said that. He is Mirsad. He is lawyer from the Ljubija mine. I also know him from around the town. We were not friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. We keep talking about some -- we are talking about measures; could you tell me how tall are you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: 183 -- no, well, I am getting on in age so I must have -- I must have become shorter by a couple of millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me approximately, without those five or six millimetres that you less [as interpreted], on the day that you arrived in Keraterm, the person who called you out and sent you to Room 1, was he shorter than you are, taller, or more or less your height?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, he could have been slightly shorter perhaps. And he was below me, and there is a slight slope and he was standing below me. That's perhaps a mistake, but thereabouts, perhaps slightly lower, perhaps. But my feeling was he was fatter, that he had round cheeks. That is the feeling that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned just now that there was a confusion or a mistake, could you tell us why did you say that? Did somebody tell you that there was a confusion or a mistake?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you said -- when you mentioned the situation about some people and the identification, the identification after the break, you answered a question that there had been a confusion or a mistake. And my question was to you: How is it that you became aware of that confusion or perhaps a mistake? Did somebody tell you something?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Do you know how this confusion arose, what I think? I agree, accept that I was mistaken, that I don't know those people. It is a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But just be brief.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Because with this Mr. Kole, I was in the loo, one on one, and Mr. Kole is shorter than I am, could be 10, 15 or as much as 15 centimetres, fair hair. That is somehow a picture I retained in my head, not particularly thick hair. Yes, it is true I am slightly colour-blind, but to me fair hair, that is how I saw it; disheveled and slightly longer with that description that I gave. Now, it was ten years ago and that is from when I was at a distance of half a metre from him. And I know it was Kole, that is, I knew the shifts. Everybody had fled. I couldn't flee because -- so that is the picture that I retain. And that man, well, perhaps I could give them a better look. Perhaps, of course, I should -- I made a mistake. Perhaps I should have stood up. But I am saying what I have said, they should have stood up so that I see how tall they are, and for me to come closer to them. Because at that distance, I don't really see well. And that is my answer true and proper. So that is a mistake in the identification. I did make this mistake. I own up to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question was very short, if you can give me a short answer. Now, you told me about this but when you became aware of your mistake, did somebody tell you this was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I realised it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Straight away?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to explain it to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No. No. You don't have to explain it to us, you've already done that.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since we were talking about that, could you tell me -- since we are at it, could you tell me how tall am I?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, you could be close to 190 I should say -- well, give or take. Yes, I'd say 190, perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Zigic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you used to see him around the camp?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did not see him because he stood on me. And I wouldn't be able to identify him, to recognise him, but he stood on me. And if you want me to, I'll explain how. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor should have asked me that. How is it that he stood on me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Tomo Prodan?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Fustar?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, by name, but not what he looks like. Perhaps I knew his father, perhaps, maybe. Perhaps his father was a Montenegrin, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us: When you mentioned Zigic, could you describe him to us, tell us what he looked like, if you remember? If you don't, then never mind.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did not see him well. I mean, I saw him in Trnopolje, in Trnopolje, during an incident when he wanted to slit somebody's throat and then guards came. They were less than five metres away from me. Well, shortish, with somewhat receding hair, dirty. Next to that old one, that is where I saw him, and in Keraterm, because he did come, and he used to come during the period of time when I was very weak. Perhaps at first he was outside, in front of the entrance, and on one occasion he was in the room. But then again, he had pushed us all, the whole lot of us, to an area about ten metres, and somebody threw a blanket or something over me and he literally stood on me. And he fired shots, not at men; at this metal contraption there. I think somebody was wounded because of this metal beam or something. He did not fire at men on that occasion. And I believe he was drunk then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it all happened in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. In Keraterm. The first case that I described was in Trnopolje, when we arrived in Trnopolje, the second or the third day after our arrival. But the first case, that is, when he stood on me, when people covered me up because they could not carry me or take me away, as it all happened very quick, and when he stood on me, that was in Keraterm, sometime in night hours. It could have been 11.00, half past. We didn't have watches because they had seized them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. And tell us, was he alone on that occasion or was he with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: He was alone. And that door was usually locked. I don't know which shift was on duty, but the door was normally locked, so somebody had let him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we must proceed. We must move on.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The man called Duca whom you mentioned, could you describe him to us?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I saw him once in daytime, but generally speaking, I did not see him. I saw him when he beat me. How shall I put this? After all that foul language. And specifically, I remember his army trousers, to begin with, his trainers, and a powerfully-built man, I mean physically strong, of about my height, give or take. Not long hair, no cap. The upper part, I don't know what he had. And I just gleaned him once in daytime, because we all fled when he appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned brothers Banovic, I remembered -- I remembered you said a metre and something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said a metre and a razor blade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but could you please explain to us better what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, they looked the same to me, even of the same height. They had long black hair. And that night the hair was loose, but at times they had it in a ponytail. A military uniform. Physically? Well, I don't know whether that look that I cast at them was realistic, because it's not really -- my sight wasn't at its best, and their blows were not really -- I mean, I know what a blow is, but I think it was amateurish. And when they came -- they also came to Trnopolje, and my children -- my elder daughter recognised them because there was a kindergarten where they lived, and the wife. I think one of them made some coffee. But I didn't know them. And one of them made coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it then true that they looked alike, that both of them had long hair which was at times tied in a ponytail, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, roughly. They changed from time to time. For instance, when my wife came, when my wife came, he was in that hut to the left as I come out from my room and walk to the ramp. He was there with Mr. Milorad, but I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, it's time for the break. Mr. Hidic, we are going to take a break until 10 minutes after 4.00. During the adjournment you are not to discuss the evidence with anybody, including the members of the Prosecution team. Mr. Rodic, before we leave, how much longer will your cross-examination be? I'm asking because obviously it would be in the interests of everybody, and in particular the interests of the witness, if we were to conclude his testimony today, because we take the Easter break until Monday, the 23rd, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I fully understand this. No, I will not take much longer after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry about my travel and what I will do. If the Court needs me and if they need me, we are here to arrive at the truth and so that what happened does not happen again. We -- that is why all of us, why we are all here today, including those men up there. This is the foremost thing in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the adjournment now until ten minutes after 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, notwithstanding the witness's generous offer to return after the Easter break, we are trying to finish, to conclude the evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is what will happen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, a short while ago, I think you mentioned a kiosk as a hut at the entrance of the camp.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did mention a structure that was next to the scales, the weigh scales, next to the -- which is when you entered through the gate to the right. It was brick at the bottom and some metal structure and that's where I spoke on the telephone on the next to last day. And there was also a kiosk that was, during the last period, a bit closer to Room 1 where I brought a pack of Lords cigarettes. But that was in the last period of my stay there, and I don't know what was there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this one kiosk which you observed was somewhere between Room 1 and this weigh scales, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in the sort of the last period. I think that it was brought in subsequent. I don't recall. But this is where I -- it was in this, inside this kiosk. There was six or seven of them there and I gave them a pack of Lords cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me, at the very entrance near that moveable gate, was there also some kind of a little hut or a kiosk?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that there was something to the left, but I'm not sure, near that moveable gate. But I spoke to my wife there and there was another commander of the guard there. Perhaps there was some change that had happened, and there may have been some change there, and he allowed this. So this soldier requested that I be allowed to talk to my wife and it was -- it could have been something then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it is also possible that there was some small kiosk-type structure there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. But there was some kind of a structure, perhaps not a kiosk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: There was some kind of a structure to the left as you entered, perhaps a metre or so away at the very entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you something, because I noticed that during your examination-in-chief when answering a question by the Prosecutor, you said this and then I think you were interrupted. You said that your wife was an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the way you said it, I understood you to have said that -- you said that you had had some kind of a problem because of that, or was there a problem in her coming, or was there a problem with her coming to see you? Could you explain something about that situation that you had.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it had to do with coming. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were arrested, whether she was able to come to visit?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, no problem. Across the street, this is what she was saying, there was a checkpoint there. She, herself, used to work in a bank, and she was Serbian. And she was much better than most of the other women in the bank and we -- she is still very good to me, and we live very well and I'm a Muslim. So she couldn't pass through. When you take the main road past the gas station, she didn't -- she couldn't get through there. And there was another checkpoint, there was some macadam road down there. It was some kind of road maintenance company there. There was something down there. I had never taken that road down there. So she tried to go even there, and they wouldn't let her through. However, the women who -- in fact, the men in the room where I was were mostly from Puharska, and their wives would bring food for them. And I have to say the truth, while Mr. Kole was there, I don't know if it was on his initiative or it was ordered to him, but the food came through. We also needed medicine. And I had -- and I am -- I am taking medicine myself. I had even received some from Germany, but I couldn't get them. So she kept trying. She was trying through the children too, but she couldn't get through and she was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When she tried to get through to you, did she mention to them where she was going and why?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. She gave them the identity card, and they would still turn her back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The people who were turning her back, did they give reasons why they were turning her back, why they were not letting her through?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Some offensive things like that she was going to go and sleep with me. I don't know these men. I think that she knew one or two of them. She was born in Prijedor. I don't know these men and I have no wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But if I understood you correctly, you did see her on the 2nd of August at the gate of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. And she came from the direction of the gas station. There was a road. I think that the commander of the guard was involved, and the guard himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To facilitate her access?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that even there was a telephone conversation. What was crucial for me at that point was the medicine, because I had a blood poisoning at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the medication help?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense that I was relatively -- I was in relatively good health. And I started recovering on my own, even though one leg was -- this part of the leg had an open wound. It was not healing, perhaps because I was trying to walk. The cut I received, the knife wound, did, but even today the leg, the muscle, is still not fully functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Milan Srdic or Mile Srdic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Srdjo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean to you --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Is that the dentist Srdjo? Is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Then it doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you can just tell me one more thing. In the light of your personal situation and circumstances and the area where you lived and worked, according to you, what kind of name is Damir?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET HIDIC
utterances.text: Some Muslims gave their sons names Damir. In Croatia, it is somewhat more frequent. The origin of the name I don't know. But, for instance, I have a cousin who is Damir, but then I have some cousins whose names are German, German in origin; for instance, Armin, which is the old Germanic god of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In closing, Mr. Hidic, I regret very much what you went through. I do not wish it on anyone. And I thank you very much for your answers. Your Honours, that concludes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are just before the Easter break, and there was a bargain that was struck earlier between Mr. Greaves and Mr. Hidic, and I would just like to add a consideration to such bargain so that it would be complete. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vucicevic. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No re-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hidic, that completes your testimony and you are discharged. Please escort --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're the Presiding Judge. Does the protocol allow me to say something as a victim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at this -- no, not at this stage. We have heard your testimony, and that's as much as we are entitled to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then according to me, there's something wrong with your protocol as concerns victims. I should be given five minutes. In regular courts, at least where we come from in the former Yugoslavia, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I will take that into account and note the complaint that you have made, and I will make the appropriate representations on your behalf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, Your Honours, those are the witnesses that we had planned to call today. I do understand that Your Honours may have some other matters for us by way of housekeeping, and you intimated there may be some other issues you want counsel to deal with. So I'm sorry. I could perhaps get another witness, but I see no profit in starting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at all, no. There wouldn't be any profit, as you say. Just to remind me, though, you have how many more witnesses? Twenty -- we have 29 working days, as far as I was able to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. In compliance with your request, we have actually checked this out, and I have asked the clerk of the Court to actually provide a list with our proposed order of witnesses, which have also been given to my learned friends. I can tell the Court now that by this list, we would have 21 or perhaps 22 viva voce witnesses, up until number 36 on the list. Thereafter, we have listed numbers 37 through to 50 as either transcript or expert witnesses, and then at the end, we do have two additional potential viva voce witnesses, one of whom we have had discussions with our learned friends, I believe it was last night, who would be, although not an expert, be introducing reports. So that would bring us up to a potential 23 further viva voce witnesses, plus whatever witnesses might be cross-examined in the event the Court rules on the transcript evidence. I might tell the Court that we've also met with the Defence with respect to some of those matters and, as I understand it, that my learned friends yesterday indicated that they want the opportunity to cross-examine, but would have no difficulty with the transcripts that we have tendered going in. That is my understanding, but you might want to clarify that with them, but we have attempted to have a meeting of the minds about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I should say that the intention of the Chamber is, after the Easter break, to work until 5.15 in the evening. That's as late as we are allowed to go. And on one day in the week, we'll stop earlier to allow for consultations between counsel and their clients, we'll stop at 4.30 one evening to allow for those consultations. But the Chamber does intend to work as hard as possible to complete the Prosecution's case by the 1st of June. We will be dealing with the transcripts as soon as we get back so that we know what we are facing in relation to those possibilities. Mr. Greaves, there is a submission that you made, or request that you made yesterday. Would you just remind the Chamber what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: at 4.39 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 23rd day of April, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
